hero.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years in prison for running illegal med spa out of backyard shed
hero.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St. Lucie has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an unlicensed medical spa out of a shed behind her home on the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive. Mena ran the business, called Miracle Hand and Spa, performing Botox injections and other cosmetic procedures without a valid medical license.

A victim came forward to Port St. Lucie Police in May 2025 after experiencing partial facial paralysis following a session in which Mena administered 62 units of Botox. The victim had been referred to Mena by coworkers who had previously used her services. When the victim reported the paralysis, Mena refunded the $325 fee and asked her to return for another injection of vitamins to reverse the problem. The paralysis persisted, prompting the victim to request proof of Mena's medical credentials. Mena provided an altered phlebotomy certificate that had expired in February 2024. She also falsely claimed to be a doctor from the Dominican Republic.

A multi-agency investigation involving Port St. Lucie Police, PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, PSL Business Tax, and the Florida Department of Health led to a search warrant at Mena's residence. Detectives found medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines, and injection devices for fillers and Botox inside the backyard shed.

Mena was convicted on multiple charges including three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of practicing medicine without an active license, fraud charges for obtaining property valued at $300 or more, and use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. The case highlights the dangers of unlicensed cosmetic procedures and the importance of verifying medical credentials before receiving treatment.

cards.headline: Community rallies to protect rare coral reef off Fort Pierce as federal decision looms
cards.body:
Dozens of Treasure Coast residents gathered at Blake Library in Martin County to support efforts to save the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef found nowhere else on Earth. The reef, located just off the coast of Fort Pierce hundreds of feet below the surface, faces an uncertain future after a federally appointed council voted to roll back longstanding protections that have safeguarded the ecosystem for decades.

The Oculina Bank is home to more than 2,000 marine species and thrives in deep, dark waters where most coral cannot survive. Scientists say trawling destroyed as much as 90% of the reef before federal protections were put in place. Dr. Grant Gilmore, a scientist who previously dove the rare reef, warned that removing habitat would devastate fish populations. "Very concerned about an ecosystem point of view, where your fish don't exist in a vacuum, they need a habitat, they need food," Gilmore said. "The coral reef was giving them habitat and food. You take that away, you don't have the fish."

Two proposals would reopen parts of the reef to shrimp trawling, following a Trump Executive order issued in April 2025 that directed eight regional councils nationwide to find ways to reinvigorate fishing industries. Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fishing Association and a generational shrimper, told local reporters he believes reopening shrimping access is essential for the struggling rock shrimp industry. Council data shows the rock shrimp industry has plummeted from over 700 trips per year in the mid-1990s to under 100 since 2010, with the number of active rock shrimpers dropping from 144 in 1996 to less than 30, and just 12 active boats in 2018.

Mark Perry, Executive Director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, joined Gilmore in urging the public to help save the reef. "Corals are in trouble worldwide. We shouldn't be destroying anymore," Gilmore said. Scientists at the gathering emphasized that the corals grow very slowly and have been there for a long time, and that snapper and grouper in the area rely on the reef ecosystem. The federal agency is preparing a final ruling on the fate of the Oculina Bank protections.

cards.headline: Florida lawmakers pass massive property tax cut that would raise homestead exemption to $250,000
cards.teaser: Florida lawmakers passed a property tax cut proposal Tuesday that would increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000 over two years. The measure requires approval from 60% of voters in November.
cards.body:
The bill would increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000 over two years, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The measure would also lower assessment caps on non-homesteaded properties from 10% to 5%. Voters must approve the proposal with 60% support in November before it can take effect.

Local experts are divided on what the ripple effects could mean for Treasure Coast residents. Real estate attorney Steve Wallace, based in Boynton Beach, raised the possibility of new fees tied to local services. "There could potentially be non-ad valorem taxes assigned to the sheriff's office, fire rescue, some of the other things. Additionally, there may be some increased fees because the only other way that the county or the local governments can derive revenue," Wallace said. CPA Paul Miller suggested businesses could end up carrying more of the financial burden to offset lost revenue.

Municipal attorney Raul Gastesi offered a different perspective, suggesting the measure could push home prices higher. "I expect home prices could actually increase because now home buyers have more money at their disposal, and that in the past has resulted in home prices going up," Gastesi said. Realtor Danielle Blake was skeptical of that theory, pointing to interest rates as a more significant barrier to sales than property taxes alone. All four experts acknowledged there are significant unknowns about how counties, municipalities and markets might respond to decreasing property tax revenue. As with any ballot measure that passes, lawmakers would need to return to Tallahassee to work out the specifics in a bill to implement the changes.

cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff's Office breaks up multi-county hardware store theft ring, over $500,000 stolen
cards.teaser: Three suspects tied to Operation Hammer Time burglarized at least 40 hardware stores across 13 Florida counties, including multiple locations in Stuart, Fort Pierce, and Jupiter.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in a retail theft ring dubbed Operation Hammer Time that targeted hardware stores across Martin, Palm Beach, and St. Lucie counties from December 2025 to April 2026. Major Ruben Romero said Johnny Batista, 19, Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39, and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31, were all involved in burglaries that hit at least 40 stores across 13 counties. The stolen goods were transported back to Miami-Dade County, where the suspects lived, to be sold. Roughly $500,000 worth of property was stolen in addition to damage caused to stores.

Hardware stores in Stuart, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce, and Jupiter were targeted, along with stores in Broward County. According to a Martin County Sheriff's Office affidavit, the crews used a sledgehammer or other blunt object to smash glass and completed the thefts within minutes, before police could arrive or alarms could be triggered. Batista is connected to the first known theft at Sewell Hardware in Stuart in December 2025.

Batista was arrested in February for vehicle theft and remains in Martin County Jail. Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, and Hernandez-Castro has a warrant out for his arrest. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased. The suspects face charges of racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, burglary of an occupied structure, and burglary of an unoccupied structure. Romero said investigators are still looking for one additional suspect and are working to connect earlier burglaries to the ring.

cards.headline: Heiress donates land to Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve to block development
cards.body:
An heiress is purchasing and donating land adjacent to the Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve in a direct effort to stop development in the area. The donated parcels will expand the protected natural area that serves as critical habitat for native Florida species.

The Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve protects one of the last remaining coastal scrub habitats on Florida's east coast. This rare ecosystem supports threatened and endangered species including the Florida scrub jay, gopher tortoise, and numerous plant species found nowhere else in the world. The preserve has been a conservation priority for environmental groups working to protect the Indian River Lagoon watershed.

The land acquisition and donation will prevent residential or commercial construction on parcels that had been at risk for development. Hobe Sound and the surrounding areas in northern Martin County have faced ongoing pressure from developers as population growth continues along the Treasure Coast. Conservation groups have worked for years to protect remaining natural areas from being converted to housing developments or commercial projects.

The donated land will become part of the public preserve, ensuring permanent protection from future development. The expansion adds to ongoing conservation efforts in Martin County to preserve natural areas that protect water quality in the Indian River Lagoon and provide habitat for native wildlife.

cards.headline: Florida Auto Insurance Rates Dropping Following 2023 Reforms
cards.body:
Florida drivers are seeing relief at the billing statement as auto insurance rates decline across the state, a development attributed to reforms enacted in 2023. The rate reductions mark a reversal of the sharp increases that made Florida one of the most expensive states for vehicle coverage in recent years.

The 2023 legislative reforms targeted longstanding issues in Florida's insurance market that had driven premiums upward. These changes addressed fraud, litigation costs, and other factors that insurance companies cited when raising rates. The reforms appear to be delivering the cost savings that lawmakers promised when the measures were debated and passed.

The declining rates affect Florida drivers statewide, offering financial relief to millions of residents who have struggled with rising transportation costs. Auto insurance is mandatory for vehicle owners in Florida, making the rate changes significant for household budgets across the state. Industry analysts have noted that Florida's unique insurance challenges, including frequent weather events and a high volume of uninsured drivers, had previously contributed to some of the nation's highest premiums.

The rate decreases represent a win for state legislators who championed the 2023 reforms as necessary to stabilize Florida's insurance market. Supporters of the legislation argued that reducing excessive litigation and cracking down on fraudulent claims would create a more sustainable pricing environment. The current trend suggests these policy changes are having their intended effect, though the long-term stability of rates will depend on continued implementation of the reforms and broader market conditions. Florida drivers renewing policies or shopping for coverage are encouraged to compare rates, as the reductions may vary by insurer and location within the state.

Beach safety remains a priority for local officials as tourism continues to be a vital part of the coastal economy. The investment in new equipment demonstrates a commitment to protecting both residents and visitors who use the beach for recreation.

The Islamic Center has remained an important part of Fort Pierce's diverse religious community, serving Muslims in St. Lucie County and the surrounding Treasure Coast area. The recovery and resilience shown by the congregation in the wake of the fire demonstrated the strength of community bonds.

Looking back at the decade since the fire allows Fort Pierce residents to consider the progress made in fostering understanding and protecting places of worship. The anniversary serves as a reminder of both the challenges faced and the community solidarity that emerged in response.

The planner's approach emphasizes thoughtful land use policies and strategic planning that can accommodate new residents while protecting the natural features that draw people to Florida in the first place. Treasure Coast communities have struggled with rapid growth in recent years, leading to concerns about traffic, overcrowded schools, and loss of green space.

Local officials and planning boards face constant pressure to approve new developments while also hearing from residents who worry about losing the small-town feel that defines many Treasure Coast communities. The planner's perspective suggests that with proper foresight and strong planning principles, growth does not have to mean destruction of quality of life.

cards.headline: 5 injured in multi-vehicle crash with fire on I-95 in Martin County

cards.body:
Five people were hospitalized Monday night after a multi-vehicle crash on Interstate 95 in Martin County that also sparked a vehicle fire. The collision occurred just before 10 p.m. on I-95 northbound near Exit 101 and Halpatiokee Regional Park in Stuart. Martin County Fire Rescue responded to the scene, where crews found one of the vehicles on fire and quickly extinguished the flames.

Two people suffered traumatic injuries and were transported to the hospital, while three others sustained minor injuries and were also taken for medical treatment. All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed while law enforcement investigated the crash. As of Tuesday morning, all lanes have reopened. The Florida Highway Patrol is handling the investigation into the cause of the collision.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce woman loses home and irreplaceable belongings in lightning strike fire

cards.body:
A Fort Pierce woman is displaced and asking for community support after a lightning strike last month destroyed her home and nearly all of her belongings. Rosa Rivera returned from getting a haircut at church when a utility worker stopped her outside and told her he believed her house was on fire. St. Lucie County Fire District crews rushed to extinguish the flames, and Rivera was told the fire was caused by a lightning strike.

Rivera lost clothes, furniture, and irreplaceable personal items, including photographs of her late son who passed away three years ago. The damage left Rivera, who is disabled and uninsured, without a place to live. She is currently staying with her nephew while she attempts to rebuild. Rivera was also recovering from neck fusion surgery the same week she lost her home.

A memorial outside the damaged home is one of the few things Rivera has left. Despite the losses, Rivera said she is grateful that she was not inside when the fire broke out. A GoFundMe has been set up to help Rivera rebuild her life and home.

cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage Tuesday of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before exiting the water and running toward nearby homes. The video, posted on the Port St. Lucie Police Department's Facebook page, shows the large bear navigating through residential waters in what officials described as seasonal behavior for Florida's black bear population.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Bear Management Program said they are monitoring the bear. If the bear does not move from the area on its own, bear biologists may set a trap to capture and relocate it. Port St. Lucie police stated that as Florida's black bears become more active this time of year in search of food, occasional sightings in residential neighborhoods can occur. According to the FWC, bear sightings remain rare throughout most of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County regions.

Wildlife officials recommend maintaining significant distance from bears, never approaching the animal, and avoiding any attempts to feed it. Port St. Lucie police advise residents to keep children and pets away from bears and secure potential food sources including garbage, pet food, and bird seed around their properties. During unexpected bear encounters, officials stress remaining calm, avoiding running, slowly backing away while keeping the bear visible, speaking in calm, firm tones, and ensuring the animal has a clear escape route.

cards.teaser: Twelve children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were sworn in as junior deputies by Sheriff Richard Del Toro, touring the facilities and seeing SWAT and K-9 demonstrations.

Twelve children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were sworn in as junior deputies by St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro on Wednesday. Sheriff Del Toro said the event was one of the greatest days in his career. The young honorees received badges, toured the sheriff's office, saw the helicopter, and watched SWAT team and K-9 demonstrations.

Among the junior deputies were twins Mia and Daryl Nyack. In 2023, Mia was diagnosed with aplastic anemia, a blood disorder, and needed a bone marrow transplant. Her twin brother Daryl donated his bone marrow to save her life, enduring time in a wheelchair and significant pain. Their mother, Melissa Nyack, said Mia was scared during the ordeal, but her brother made her feel safe.

Deleon said she is grateful that local heroes made her son feel special and reminded the children that they are important members of the community. Sheriff Del Toro said the children left an imprint on the department and made their wish come true.

cards.headline: Raising Cane's to open two new Florida locations

cards.headline: Florida lawmakers advance property tax overhaul with potential impact on local children's services
cards.teaser: The Florida legislature has approved changes to property tax policy that critics warn could affect funding for children's services across the state, including the Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
State lawmakers have passed a significant property tax overhaul that will place a constitutional amendment on the ballot for voters to decide. The proposal expands the homestead property tax exemption, which would reduce the amount of property tax revenue collected by local governments.

Critics of the measure argue the tax cuts could dismantle what they describe as a children's safety net by reducing funding available for local services. Counties across Florida, including Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River, rely heavily on property tax revenue to fund schools, libraries, parks, and social services that benefit families and children.

The proposed changes have sparked debate among Florida lawmakers about the balance between providing tax relief to homeowners and maintaining adequate funding for local government services. Voters will ultimately decide whether to approve the constitutional amendment in an upcoming election.

Local government officials have raised concerns about how reduced property tax revenue would impact funding for fire departments, law enforcement, road maintenance, and other services that residents rely on daily. The debate has put lawmakers in a difficult position as they try to provide tax relief to residents facing rising home values and insurance costs while ensuring that cities and counties can continue to deliver the services their communities expect. cards.headline: Legislature approves expanded homestead exemption, sends constitutional amendment to voters
cards.teaser: The Florida legislature has approved an expansion of the homestead property tax exemption, which will appear as a constitutional amendment on an upcoming ballot.
cards.body:
State lawmakers have given final approval to legislation that would expand Florida's homestead property tax exemption, placing the question before voters as a constitutional amendment in an upcoming election. The measure represents a significant change to how property taxes are calculated for Florida homeowners.

The homestead exemption currently allows homeowners to reduce the taxable value of their primary residence, providing tax relief. The proposed expansion would increase this exemption, resulting in lower property tax bills for eligible homeowners across the state, including those on the Treasure Coast.

If voters approve the constitutional amendment, local governments will collect less property tax revenue, which could require adjustments to budgets and service levels. County commissioners, school boards, and city councils would need to decide whether to cut spending, find alternative revenue sources, or adjust millage rates to compensate for the reduced tax base.

cards.headline: Lake Worth Beach to host 80-mile ocean paddle raising funds for cystic fibrosis
cards.teaser: More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of open Atlantic Ocean from the Bahamas to Lake Worth Beach on June 13, raising awareness and funds for families living with cystic fibrosis.
cards.body:
Lake Worth Beach will serve as the finish line for an endurance paddle crossing on June 13 when more than 100 participants complete an 80-mile journey from Bimini, Bahamas. The annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis will see paddlers launch at midnight and arrive at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. Event founder Travis Suit created the crossing to benefit the Pipers Angels Foundation, which he established after his daughter Piper was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

The four-day event begins June 10 with arrivals in Bimini and includes a 4Ocean beach cleanup, a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony honoring cystic fibrosis warriors, and mandatory safety meetings. All paddlers must wear U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices, waterproof whistles, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers will be provided and must remain active throughout the crossing. Participants must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, with crew and virtual participants having a $500 minimum. Final contributions are due July 31.

Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 for a daylong beach celebration to cheer paddlers as they arrive. The event not only raises funds but also spotlights ongoing needs for research, treatment, and family support for cystic fibrosis, a life-shortening genetic condition affecting the lungs and digestive system. More information, registration, and donation details are available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

cards.headline: Beetlejuice the musical runs through June 7 at West Palm Beach's Kravis Center
cards.teaser: The Broadway hit musical Beetlejuice brings spooky humor and over-the-top visuals to the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach, with performances running through June 7.
cards.body:
Beetlejuice the musical is now playing at the Kravis Center's Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall in West Palm Beach through June 7. The Broadway production stars actor Ryan Stajmiger in the iconic striped suit of the mischievous demon made famous by Michael Keaton in Tim Burton's 1988 film. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a strange and unusual teen whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is breaking the fourth wall and communicating directly with the audience. He shared that early in the run, a wig change went awry when both wigs came off at once, leaving him bald for an entire scene. The unexpected moment became part of the performance as he played with the situation and the audience's reaction.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50 and are available at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up with parental discretion advised. The production is part of the Kravis Center's continuing effort to bring major Broadway shows to Palm Beach County, offering residents big-stage experiences and boosting the region as a cultural destination.

hero.headline: Florida Auto Insurance Rates Dropping Following 2023 Reforms
hero.body:
Florida drivers are seeing relief at the billing statement as auto insurance rates decline across the state, a development attributed to reforms enacted in 2023. The rate reductions mark a reversal of the sharp increases that made Florida one of the most expensive states for vehicle coverage in recent years.

The 2023 legislative reforms targeted longstanding issues in Florida's insurance market that had driven premiums upward. These changes addressed fraud, litigation costs, and other factors that insurance companies cited when raising rates. The reforms appear to be delivering the cost savings that lawmakers promised when the measures were debated and passed.

The declining rates affect Florida drivers statewide, offering financial relief to millions of residents who have struggled with rising transportation costs. Auto insurance is mandatory for vehicle owners in Florida, making the rate changes significant for household budgets across the state. Industry analysts have noted that Florida's unique insurance challenges, including frequent weather events and a high volume of uninsured drivers, had previously contributed to some of the nation's highest premiums.

The rate decreases represent a win for state legislators who championed the 2023 reforms as necessary to stabilize Florida's insurance market. Supporters of the legislation argued that reducing excessive litigation and cracking down on fraudulent claims would create a more sustainable pricing environment. The current trend suggests these policy changes are having their intended effect, though the long-term stability of rates will depend on continued implementation of the reforms and broader market conditions. Florida drivers renewing policies or shopping for coverage are encouraged to compare rates, as the reductions may vary by insurer and location within the state.

hero.headline: Multi-county hardware store theft ring hits Stuart and Fort Pierce, 3 arrested in Operation Hammer Time
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in a retail theft operation that targeted hardware stores across the region, including locations in Stuart and Fort Pierce. Major Ruben Romero said Johnny Batista, 19, Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39, and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31 were involved in a series of burglaries at hardware stores across Martin, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties from December 2025 to April 2026.

At least 40 stores across 13 counties were burglarized, with stolen goods taken back to Miami-Dade County where the suspects lived to be sold. Roughly $500,000 worth of property was stolen, in addition to damage to stores. According to the affidavit from Martin County Sheriff's Office, hardware stores in Stuart, Fort Pierce, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, West Palm Beach and Jupiter were targeted, as were stores in Broward County.

The crews used a sledgehammer or other blunt object to smash the glass and often completed the thefts within minutes, before police arrived or alarms were triggered. Investigators say Batista is connected to the first known theft at Sewell Hardware in Stuart in December 2025. Romero said the thefts impact the entire community through higher costs. "There's already inflation that we notice severely in our state, and the more they steal, the more damage they cause, the more expensive things are. People can't go to work because they can't afford the tools."

Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, Batista was arrested in February for a vehicle theft and is in Martin County Jail, and Hernandez-Castro has a warrant out for his arrest. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased. The suspects are facing charges of racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, burglary of an occupied structure and burglary of an unoccupied structure. Romero said there are burglaries that happened previous to December, and investigators are still looking for one other suspect.

Five people were hospitalized Monday night after a multi-vehicle crash on Interstate 95 that also sparked a vehicle fire, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The collision occurred just before 10 p.m. on I-95 northbound near Exit 101 and Halpatiokee Regional Park. Martin County Fire Rescue responded to the scene, where they found one of the vehicles on fire and quickly extinguished the flames.

Two people suffered traumatic injuries and were transported to the hospital, while three others sustained minor injuries and were also taken for medical treatment. All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed while law enforcement investigated the crash. As of Tuesday morning, all lanes have reopened.

The Florida Highway Patrol is conducting the investigation into the crash. The incident caused significant traffic disruptions for commuters traveling northbound through Martin County Monday night.

cards.headline: Activists rally at Blake Library to save rare Oculina coral reef off Fort Pierce from shrimp trawling
cards.teaser: Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County after a federally appointed council voted to roll back longstanding protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef found nowhere else on Earth.
cards.body:
Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County after a federally appointed council voted to roll back longstanding protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef found nowhere else on Earth. Located just off the coast of Fort Pierce, the reef is hidden hundreds of feet below the surface. Unlike most coral that needs shallow sunlight to survive, the Oculina Bank thrives in deep, dark waters and is home to more than 2,000 marine species.

Two proposals would reopen parts of the reef to shrimp trawling even though scientists say trawling destroyed as much as 90% of the reef before federal protections were put in place decades ago. Dr. Grant Gilmore, a scientist who previously dived the rare reef, said the coral reef provides essential habitat and food for fish. "Very concerned about an ecosystem point of view, where your fish don't exist in a vacuum, they need a habitat, they need food. The coral reef was giving them habitat and food. You take that away, you don't have the fish." Mark Perry, Executive Director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, and Gilmore urged the public to help save the reef at the gathering.

The proposals followed a Trump Executive order issued in April of 2025 that tasked the eight regional councils nationwide to find ways to reinvigorate the fishing industries. Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fishing Association and a generational shrimper, believes reopening shrimping access to the Oculina Bank is essential for the struggling rock shrimp industry. Council data shows the rock shrimp industry has plummeted from over 700 trips per year in the mid-1990s to under 100 since 2010. The number of active rock shrimpers dropped from 144 in 1996 to less than 30, with just 12 active boats in 2018.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce woman loses home and irreplaceable photos of late son after lightning strike

hero.body:

St. Lucie County District Firefighters responded to extinguish the flames, but the damage had already been done.

Rivera lost clothes, furniture, and irreplaceable personal belongings including photographs of her late son who passed away three years ago. The displaced resident is now staying at her nephew's home while she tries to rebuild. Rivera is uninsured and was recovering from neck fusion surgery the same week she lost her home, making the situation especially difficult for the disabled woman.

A memorial outside the damaged home remains one of the few things Rivera has that cannot be replaced. Despite the overwhelming loss, Rivera expressed gratitude that she was not inside when the fire broke out. A GoFundMe has been set up to help Rivera rebuild her life after the disaster.

cards.headline: Black bear spotted swimming through Port St. Lucie neighborhood in rare Treasure Coast sighting
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police shared video footage of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before running toward nearby homes. Wildlife officials say the bear is being monitored and may be trapped and relocated if it doesn't leave on its own.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police shared rare video footage Tuesday of a black bear swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community before exiting the water and running toward nearby homes. The large black bear was captured on video navigating through residential waters in what officials described as seasonal behavior for Florida's black bear population.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Bear Management Program said they are monitoring the bear. If it doesn't move from the area on its own, bear biologists may set a trap to capture and relocate it. According to the FWC, bear sightings remain rare throughout most of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County regions, making Tuesday's Port St. Lucie encounter particularly noteworthy for local residents.

Port St. Lucie police stated that as Florida's black bears become more active this time of year in search of food, occasional sightings in residential neighborhoods can occur. Wildlife officials advise residents to maintain significant distance from bears, never approach them, keep children and pets away, and secure potential food sources including garbage, pet food, and bird seed around their properties. If encountering a bear, residents should remain calm, avoid running, slowly back away while keeping the bear visible, and ensure the animal has a clear escape route.

cards.headline: Historic Boston House in Fort Pierce reopens as downtown dining destination after renovation
cards.teaser: The Boston House, a Fort Pierce landmark built in 1909 along South Indian River Drive, has officially reopened as a new dining experience. The National Register of Historic Places building was carefully renovated to preserve its past while serving the downtown area.
cards.body:
A historic Fort Pierce landmark is entering a new chapter as the Boston House reopens as a downtown dining destination. Built in 1909 along South Indian River Drive, the home is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and has served a variety of roles over the decades. Now, its newest owners are working to preserve its past while reimagining its purpose.

Co-owner Georgette Angelos said she wants guests to feel at home automatically while honoring the building's legacy. Originally built by an engineer for Henry Flagler's Florida East Coast Railway who later became St. Lucie County's third sheriff, the Boston House remains closely tied to the region's early development. During renovations, the owners intentionally preserved historic details including low original ceilings and Florida-themed law books that nod to the home's past.

General manager Scott Laird said the revival of the property reflects broader momentum downtown. Fort Pierce has worked to bring new life to the downtown area, and each room in the Boston House offers a distinct experience rooted in local history. The reopening stands as both a historic landmark and a renewed gathering place serving up a new chapter for downtown Fort Pierce.

cards.headline: 12 Make-A-Wish children sworn in as junior deputies at St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office
cards.teaser: Twelve kids from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were sworn in as junior deputies by Sheriff Richard Del Toro on Wednesday, including twins Mia and Daryl who share a remarkable story of survival and sacrifice.
cards.body:
Twelve kids from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were honored by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office on Wednesday, sworn in as junior deputies by Sheriff Richard Del Toro. The sheriff called it one of the greatest days in his career as the children received badges, toured the sheriff's office, and saw helicopter, SWAT team, and K-9 demonstrations.

Among the newest junior deputies were twins Mia and Daryl. In 2023, Mia was diagnosed with aplastic anemia, a blood disorder that required a bone marrow transplant. Her twin brother Daryl donated his bone marrow to save his sister's life, enduring a wheelchair and significant pain during the process. Mia said she was scared, but her brother made her feel safe. Another junior deputy, Tobias, was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia in 2022. His mother Charity Deleon said things that don't normally happen to a child happened to him, and they even lost him at one point before medical staff were able to bring him back and he miraculously recovered.

Deleon thanked the sheriff's office for making the time and energy to welcome the children into the community and remind them that they're important. Sheriff Del Toro said these heroes left an imprint on the department, telling the children they made the sheriff's office's wish come true.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years in prison for running illegal med spa out of backyard shed
cards.teaser: Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St.
cards.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St. Lucie has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an unlicensed medical spa called Miracle Hand and Spa from a shed behind her home on the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive. A victim who experienced partial facial paralysis after receiving 62 units of Botox injections from Mena came to police in May 2025, triggering a multi-agency investigation that uncovered extensive illegal medical operations.

The victim, who was referred to the business by coworkers, paid $325 for the services. When she reported the paralysis, Mena refunded the money and asked her to return for another injection of vitamins to reverse the issues. After the paralysis continued, the victim requested to see Mena's medical license. Mena provided an altered certificate of phlebotomy that had actually expired in February 2024. Mena also told the victim she was a doctor from the Dominican Republic.

Port St. Lucie Police worked with PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, PSL Business Tax, and the Florida Department of Health to execute a search warrant at Mena's residence. Detectives found medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines, and injection devices for fillers and Botox.

Mena was charged with three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of health safety practicing medicine without an active license, one count of fraud-swindle obtain property $300 or more, one count of fraud-swindle obtain property under $20,000, and one count of use of two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. The investigation involved multiple agencies working together to shut down the illegal operation that had been serving multiple clients in the Port St. Lucie area.
